q: With him was joined his son Lausus, a generous youth worthy of a better sire.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aeneas is destined to lead Etruscans (as a foreign leader appointed by fate)
q: You, equally by birth and time of life, and fame in arms, pointed out by the gods, have but to appear to be hailed as their leader.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Etruscans inhabit country beyond the river (across the Tiber from Evander's state)
q: The Etruscans hold the country beyond the river.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Etruscans oppose Mezentius (demanding his surrender for punishment)
q: The Etruscans' demand that he shall be given up to deserved punishment

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Etruscans offer leadership to Aeneas (because their priests require a foreign leader)
q: You, equally by birth and time of life, and fame in arms, pointed out by the gods, have but to appear to be hailed as their leader.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Etruscans is led by Tarchon (during the alliance against Turnus)
q: AEneas and his band safely arrived at the Etruscan camp and were received with open arms by Tarchon, the Etruscan leader, and his countrymen.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: alliance between Aeneas and Latinus is granted by Latinus (after the Trojan embassy is favorably received)
q: Latinus immediately concluded that the Trojan hero was no other than the promised son-in-law announced by the oracle. He cheerfully granted his alliance

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: oracle concerning Lavinia's marriage foretells foreign husband for Lavinia (revealed to Latinus through Faunus in a dream)
q: Latinus had been warned in a dream by his father Faunus, that the destined husband of Lavinia should come from a foreign land.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: oracle concerning Lavinia's marriage foretells world-subduing race (to spring from Lavinia's marriage)
q: From that union should spring a race destined to subdue the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Latinus is a king (ruler of the country)
q: Latinus, third in descent from Saturn, ruled the country.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Latinus is descended from Kronos (third in descent)
q: Latinus, third in descent from Saturn, ruled the country.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Latinus has child Lavinia (his only described child)
q: He was now old and had no male descendant, but had one charming daughter, Lavinia, who was sought in marriage by many neighboring chiefs

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Latinus favors marriage between Lavinia (with Turnus)
q: one of whom, Turnus, king of the Rutulians, was favored by the wishes of her parents.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Nisus stands guard at the entrance of the camp
q: Nisus stood guard at the entrance of the camp

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Turnus fights with Aeneas (in the final conflict)
q: At length the final conflict took place between AEneas and Turnus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aeneas is a Trojan hero
q: The Trojan hero then threw his, which penetrated the shield of Turnus, and pierced his thigh.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aeneas commands Trojans
q: having received strict orders from AEneas not to fight in his absence

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aeneas is protected by Vulcan's armor (impenetrable armor fabricated at Venus's request)
q: On the side of AEneas were the expressed decree of destiny, the aid of his goddess-mother at every emergency, and impenetrable armor fabricated by Vulcan, at Venus' request, for her son.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aeneas marries Lavinia (after triumphing over his foes)
q: Here the AEneid closes, but the story goes that AEneas, having triumphed over his foes, obtained Lavinia as his bride.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Trojans has camp camp
q: In the camp of the Trojans things were far otherwise.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Trojans occupies Trojan camp
q: In the camp of the Trojans things were far otherwise.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Nisus guards Trojan camp (at its entrance)
q: Nisus stood guard at the entrance of the camp

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Mezentius is a tyrant
q: The tyrant Mezentius, finding himself engaged against his revolted subjects, raged like a wild beast.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Mezentius is opposed by revolted subjects of Mezentius (in battle)
q: finding himself engaged against his revolted subjects

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Mezentius is father of Lausus
q: Lausus, his son, could not bear the sight, but rushed forward and interposed himself

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Mezentius possesses Mezentius's horse (used in battle against Aeneas)
q: He mounted his horse and dashed into the thickest of the fight, seeking AEneas.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lausus is a son of Mezentius
q: Lausus, his son, could not bear the sight, but rushed forward and interposed himself

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Nisus is friend of Euryalus (and brother in arms)
q: These two were friends and brothers in arms.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lausus is bent over by Aeneas (in pity)
q: Lausus fell, and AEneas bent over him in pity.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pallas is a youthful champion (brave but unequally matched against Turnus)
q: The contest between champions so unequally matched could not be doubtful. Pallas bore himself bravely, but fell by the lance of Turnus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pallas is killed by Turnus (in battle)
q: Pallas bore himself bravely, but fell by the lance of Turnus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pallas's belt is a belt (adorned with studs and carvings of gold)
q: The belt only, adorned with studs and carvings of gold, he took and clasped round his own body.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Camilla is a virgin warrior (chiefly conspicuous in battle)
q: Another battle ensued, in which Camilla, the virgin warrior, was chiefly conspicuous.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Camilla uses Camilla's battle-axe (in battle)
q: many Trojans and Etruscans fell pierced with her darts or struck down by her battle-axe.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Camilla uses Camilla's darts (in battle)
q: many Trojans and Etruscans fell pierced with her darts or struck down by her battle-axe.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Aruns kills Camilla (with a javelin)
q: the javelin of Aruns struck her and inflicted a fatal wound.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Nisus is older than Euryalus
q: You are younger than I and have more of life in prospect.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Lavinia is wife of Aeneas (obtained as his bride after his triumph)
q: AEneas, having triumphed over his foes, obtained Lavinia as his bride.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Alba Longa is founded by Iulus
q: His son Iulus founded the city of Alba Longa.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Alba Longa is ruled by Iulus's descendants (for many years)
q: He, and his descendants after him, reigned over the town for many years.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Rhea Silvia is a Vestal Virgin (appointed to celibacy)
q: Amulius seized the crown by force, cast out Numitor, and made his daughter, Rhea Silvia, a Vestal Virgin.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Rhea Silvia is mother of Romulus (by Mars)
q: But Rhea Silvia broke her vow, and gave birth, by the god Mars, to the twins, Romulus and Remus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Rhea Silvia is mother of Remus (by Mars)
q: But Rhea Silvia broke her vow, and gave birth, by the god Mars, to the twins, Romulus and Remus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Rhea Silvia is punished by burial alive of Rhea Silvia (for breaking her vow as a Vestal)
q: For this offence she was buried alive, the usual punishment accorded to unfaithful Vestals

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Romulus is a twin son of Rhea Silvia (by Mars)
q: But Rhea Silvia broke her vow, and gave birth, by the god Mars, to the twins, Romulus and Remus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Romulus is brother of Remus (as a twin)
q: to the twins, Romulus and Remus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Romulus founds Rome (with Remus)
q: Afterwards they founded, by the side of the river Tiber, where they had been exposed in infancy, the city of Rome.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Euryalus is a youth (distinguished above all in the army for graces of person and fine qualities)
q: Euryalus, a youth distinguished above all in the army for graces of person and fine qualities, was with him.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Remus is a twin son of Rhea Silvia (by Mars)
q: But Rhea Silvia broke her vow, and gave birth, by the god Mars, to the twins, Romulus and Remus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Remus is brother of Romulus (as a twin)
q: to the twins, Romulus and Remus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Tiber is a river
q: the children were exposed on the river Tiber.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: exposure of Romulus and Remus occurs at Tiber (in infancy)
q: the children were exposed on the river Tiber.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: exposure of Romulus and Remus is followed by rescue by herdsman
q: Romulus and Remus, however, were rescued by a herdsman

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Euryalus is friend of Nisus (and brother in arms)
q: These two were friends and brothers in arms.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Euryalus is child of Euryalus's mother (his aged mother)
q: My aged mother is with me in the camp.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Euryalus is pierced by the sword (in the comely bosom)
q: While he spoke the sword fell, and pierced the comely bosom of Euryalus.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras is native of the island of Samos (born, perhaps, about five hundred and forty years B.C.)
q: Pythagoras (born, perhaps, about five hundred and forty years B.C.) was a native of the island of Samos, but passed the chief portion of his life at Crotona in Italy.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras has disciples six hundred of the inhabitants (enrolled in a society to aid each other in the pursuit of wisdom)
q: Six hundred of the inhabitants became his disciples and enrolled themselves in a society to aid each other in the pursuit of wisdom; uniting their property in one common stock, for the benefit of the whole.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoreans regard silence as first lesson (novices were initially hearers only)
q: The first lesson they learned was SILENCE; for a time they were required to be only hearers.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoreans accept Pythagoras's authority (“He (Pythagoras) said so” was treated as sufficient without proof)
q: "He (Pythagoras) said so," (Ipse dixit,) was to be held by them as sufficient, without any proof.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras regards numbers as essence and principle of all things
q: Pythagoras is said to have considered NUMBERS as the essence and principle of all things, and attributed to them a real and distinct existence; so that, in his view, they were the elements out of which the universe was constructed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Monad is a unit (the source of all numbers)
q: The "Monad," or UNIT, he regarded as the source of all numbers.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras regards Monad (as the source of all numbers)
q: The "Monad," or UNIT, he regarded as the source of all numbers.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: metempsychosis is a doctrine of the transmigration of souls (connected with reward and punishment of human actions)
q: This doctrine of the transmigration of souls (metempsychosis), which was first Indian and Egyptian, and connected with the doctrine of reward and punishment of human actions

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras is native to Samos
q: Pythagoras (born, perhaps, about five hundred and forty years B.C.) was a native of the island of Samos, but passed the chief portion of his life at Crotona in Italy.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: metempsychosis holds that souls are immortal (souls pass between human and animal bodies)
q: Souls never die, but always on quitting one abode pass to another.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoreans kill animals no animals (because of metempsychosis)
q: This doctrine of the transmigration of souls (metempsychosis), which was first Indian and Egyptian, and connected with the doctrine of reward and punishment of human actions, was the chief cause why the Pythagoreans killed no animals.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: lyre is invented by Pythagoras (according to one tradition)
q: Pythagoras is said to have invented the lyre, of which other fables give the invention to Mercury.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Sybaris is a city (neighboring Crotona and proverbial for luxury and effeminacy)
q: Sybaris, a neighboring city to Crotona, was as celebrated for luxury and effeminacy as Crotona for the reverse.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Sybaris is destroyed by Crotona (after being conquered in war)
q: A war arose between the two cities, and Sybaris was conquered and destroyed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Crotona is a city (noted for sobriety in contrast with Sybaris)
q: Sybaris, a neighboring city to Crotona, was as celebrated for luxury and effeminacy as Crotona for the reverse.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras lives at Crotona (for the chief portion of his life)
q: Pythagoras (born, perhaps, about five hundred and forty years B.C.) was a native of the island of Samos, but passed the chief portion of his life at Crotona in Italy.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Milo leads Crotona
q: Milo, the celebrated athlete, led the army of Crotona.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Champollion the younger discovers Egyptian hieroglyphics (first opened their secret to modern times)
q: The remarkable discovery by which Champollion the younger (so called to distinguish him from his older brother, Champollion Figeac, who also studied the hieroglyphics)) first opened to modern times the secret of the Egyptian hieroglyphics

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian religion is a religion (its theology varied across periods and schools)
q: It is impossible, because that theology was different in one time and with one school from what it was at other times.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian religion has polytheistic local groups (according to S. Birch)
q: Mr. S. Birch, of the British Museum, says, "The religion of the Egyptians consisted of an extended polytheism represented by a system of local groups."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian religion is interpreted as manifestations of one being (according to Pierret)
q: But Mr. Pierret says, "The polytheism of the monuments is but an outward show. The innumerable gods of the Pantheon are but manifestations of the One Being in his various capacities.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian religion has foundation in pantheism (according to Mariette Bey)
q: Mariette Bey says, "The one result is that according to the Egyptians, the universe was God himself, and that Pantheism formed the foundation of their religion."

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian triads are a male deity, female deity, and child (successive manifestations of the original divinity)
q: These forms are generally triads, and resolve themselves into a male deity, a female deity, and their child.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Osiris is opposed by Set (Set is the Egyptian devil)
q: Mr. Birch believes that the worship of Osiris prevailed largely beside the worship of the Sun, and is not to be confounded with it. To Osiris, Set, the Egyptian devil, was opposed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras travels to Egypt (according to tradition, where he was instructed by the priests)
q: When young he travelled extensively and is said to have visited Egypt, where he was instructed by the priests in all their learning

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Osiris is a god of the lower world (judge of the dead and representative of the sun below the horizon)
q: OSIRIS: Of human form, mummified, crowned with a mitre, and holding the flail and crook. Called the Good; the Lord above all; the one lord. Was the god of the lower world; judge of the dead; and representative of the sun below the horizon.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Set is a symbol of evil (in later times and enemy of Osiris)
q: Was originally a warlike god, and became in later times the symbol of evil and the enemy of Osiris.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Horus is a son of Osiris
q: Horus or Harpocrates, named above, was the son of Osiris.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Horus is worshipped at Apollinopolis Magna (as local deity of Edfoo)
q: Local deity of Edfoo (Apollinopolis Magna).

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Jupiter Ammon is a chief deity of Thebes (king of the gods; the concealed sun)
q: AMEN RA: Of human form, crowned with a flat-topped cap and two long, straight plumes; clothed in the schenti; his flesh sometimes painted blue. There are various forms of this god (there were almost as many varieties of Ammon in Egypt as there are varieties of the Madonna in Italy or Spain), but he is most generally described as King of the Gods, chief deity of Thebes.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ra is a sun deity (divine disposer and organizer of the world)
q: RA: Hawk-headed, and crowned with the sun-disc, encircled by an asp. The divine disposer and organizer of the world; adored throughout Egypt.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Isis is worshipped at Abydos (her soul was believed to reside in Sothis)
q: ISIS: A woman crowned with the sun-disc surmounted by a throne, and sometimes enclosed between horns. Adored at Abydos. Her soul resided in Sothis on the Dog-star.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian hieroglyphics are deciphered by Champollion the younger (their secret was opened to modern times)
q: The remarkable discovery by which Champollion the younger (so called to distinguish him from his older brother, Champollion Figeac, who also studied the hieroglyphics)) first opened to modern times the secret of the Egyptian hieroglyphics

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Egyptian hieroglyphics are found on monuments (along with manuscripts in tombs)
q: The latest modern literature occasionally uses the Egyptian names, as the last two centuries have disinterred them from the inscriptions on the monuments, and from the manuscripts in the tombs.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras visits Chaldean Magi (during his eastern journey)
q: and afterwards journeyed to the East, and visited the Persian and Chaldean Magi, and the Brahmins of India.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras visits Brahmins of India (during his eastern journey)
q: and afterwards journeyed to the East, and visited the Persian and Chaldean Magi, and the Brahmins of India.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras leaves writings none preserved
q: But Pythagoras left no writings which have been preserved.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras establishes himself at Crotona (finally)
q: At Crotona, where he finally established himself, it is said that his extraordinary qualities collected round him a great number of disciples.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pythagoras influences Crotona (his influence produced sobriety and temperance)
q: The inhabitants were notorious for luxury and licentiousness, but the good effects of his influence were soon visible. Sobriety and temperance succeeded.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ovid is a Roman poet
q: The Roman poet Ovid gives us a connected narrative of creation.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: human race has upright stature (unlike other animals)
q: man was made in the image of the gods with an upright stature [The two Greek words for man have the root an, "up], so that while all other animals turn their faces downward and look to the earth, he raises his face to heaven and gazes on the stars

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Prometheus is a Titan (son of Iapetus and Themis)
q: Prometheus, the Titan son of Iapetus and Themis, is a favorite subject with the poets.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Epimetheus is a brother of Prometheus
q: To Prometheus the Titan and to his brother Epimetheus was committed the task of making man and all other animals, and of endowing them with all needful faculties.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Prometheus is committed task of making man and all other animals (with Epimetheus)
q: To Prometheus the Titan and to his brother Epimetheus was committed the task of making man and all other animals, and of endowing them with all needful faculties.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Epimetheus gives animals' faculties (including courage, strength, swiftness, sagacity, wings, claws, and shelly coverings)
q: Epimetheus then gave to the different animals their several gifts of courage, strength, swiftness and sagacity. He gave wings to one, claws to another, a shelly covering to the third.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Prometheus brings fire (from heaven to man)
q: Prometheus, with the aid of Minerva, went up to heaven, lighted his torch at the chariot of the sun, and brought down fire to man.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: fire enables human race (to make weapons and tools, warm dwellings, and resist cold)
q: Fire enabled him to make weapons to subdue wild beasts, tools with which to till the earth. With fire he warmed his dwelling and bid defiance to the cold.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Jupiter makes Pandora (to punish Prometheus, Epimetheus, and man)
q: The story is, that Jupiter made her, and sent her to Prometheus and his brother, to punish them for their presumption in stealing fire from heaven; and man, for accepting the gift.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora is a first woman (made in heaven)
q: The first woman was named Pandora. She was made in heaven, every god contributing something to perfect her.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora receives beauty (from Venus)
q: Venus gave her beauty, Mercury persuasion, Apollo music.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Chaos is a rough heap of inert weight and discordant beginnings (before creation was ordered)
q: Before the earth and sea and the all-covering heaven, one aspect, which we call Chaos, covered all the face of Nature,-- a rough heap of inert weight and discordant beginnings of things clashing together.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora receives persuasion (from Mercury)
q: Venus gave her beauty, Mercury persuasion, Apollo music.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora receives music (from Apollo)
q: Venus gave her beauty, Mercury persuasion, Apollo music.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora is presented to Epimetheus (on earth)
q: Thus equipped, she was conveyed to earth, and presented to Epimetheus, who gladly accepted her, though cautioned by his brother to beware of Jupiter and his gifts.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora's jar contains noxious articles (kept in Epimetheus's house)
q: Epimetheus had in his house a jar, in which were kept certain noxious articles, for which, in fitting man for his new abode, he had had no occasion.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Pandora's jar contains plagues (released when Pandora opened it)
q: Forthwith there escaped a multitude of plagues for hapless man,-- such as gout, rheumatism, and colic for his body, and envy, spite, and revenge for his mind,-- and scattered themselves far and wide.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: hope remains in Pandora's jar (as the sole thing left after the other contents escaped)
q: The whole contents of the jar had escaped, one thing only excepted, which lay at the bottom, and that was HOPE.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: hope is lasting consolation (despite other evils)
q: whatever evils are abroad, hope never entirely leaves us; and while we have THAT, no amount of other ills can make us completely wretched.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Golden Age is a age of innocence and happiness (the first age of the world)
q: The world being thus furnished with inhabitants, the first age was an age of innocence and happiness, called the GOLDEN AGE.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Golden Age is characterized by truth and right (not enforced by law or magistrates)
q: Truth and right prevailed, though not enforced by law, nor was there any magistrate to threaten or punish.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Golden Age has perpetual spring (with natural abundance)
q: Perpetual spring reigned, flowers sprang up without seed, the rivers flowed with milk and wine, and yellow honey distilled from the oaks.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: God and Nature separates Earth (from sea and heaven)
q: God and Nature at last interposed and put an end to this discord, separating earth from sea, and heaven from both.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Jupiter summons gods (to a council concerning the earth)
q: He summoned the gods to council. They obeyed the call, and took The road to the palace of heaven.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Jupiter intends to destroy human race (because of the earth's corruption)
q: Jupiter addressed the assembly. He set forth the frightful condition of things on the earth, and closed by announcing his intention to destroy the whole of its inhabitants, and provide a new race

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: flood is a means of destroying the world (chosen instead of fire)
q: but recollecting the danger that such a conflagration might set heaven itself on fire, he changed his plan, and resolved to drown the world.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: God and Nature separates the sea (from earth and heaven)
q: God and Nature at last interposed and put an end to this discord, separating earth from sea, and heaven from both.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Boreas is a north wind (chained up during the flood)
q: Aquilo, the north wind, which scatters the clouds, was chained up

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Neptune aids Jupiter (by releasing the rivers and waters)
q: Jupiter, not satisfied with his own waters, calls on his brother Neptune to aid him with his. He lets loose the rivers, and pours them over the land.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Triton serves Neptune (by sounding the retreat of the waters)
q: Neptune also directed Triton to blow on his shell, and sound a retreat to the waters.
